results.note: Demonstration on UCI German Credit; Lending Club has no protected attributes.
results.data_quality_warning: german.doc labels attribute 9 (personal status and sex) wrongly. The corrected code table published with the South German Credit data (Groemping 2019, Report 4/2019, Beuth University of Applied Sciences Berlin; UCI 2020, doi:10.24432/C5QG88) has the same row counts per code and gives: A91 male divorced/separated, A92 female non-single or male single, A93 male married/widowed, A94 female single. The 'sex' comparison follows german.doc (the convention in most fairness work) and so groups some single women as male and some single men as female; treat it as a demonstration of the method, not a measurement of sex disparity. 'sex_corrected_codes' uses only the unambiguous codes.
caveats: Small test set: 300 rows, and the smallest test group in any comparison has 25 people, so confidence intervals are wide and a point estimate below 0.8 is weak evidence on its own.

Fairness through unawareness: sex, age and foreign-worker status are not model features, but other features can act as proxies (see proxy_check). Excluding a protected attribute does not remove proxy effects.
Attribute 9 mixes sex with marital status, and german.doc mislabels it (see data_quality_warning).
The data has 1000 loans from one German bank, 1973 to 1975 (UCI South German Credit page); it says nothing about any current lending population.

Groups can differ in their observed good rates (see observed_good_rate per group), so a gap in approval rates may partly reflect that; AIR alone cannot separate risk differences from unfair treatment.

regulatory_context.four_fifths_rule: Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures, 29 CFR 1607.4(D) (1978). An employment-selection rule of thumb, used here only as a screening statistic.
regulatory_context.us_fair_lending: Equal Credit Opportunity Act, 15 U.S.C. 1691 (1974), and Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.2(z), list sex, marital status and age among prohibited bases.
regulatory_context.applicability: The German Credit data is from a German bank and is not subject to US law. Which tests apply depends on the institution and its risk profile. This is a demonstration, not a compliance program or a legal finding.

results.dataset: freMTPL2freq (OpenML 41214), public French motor third-party liability data
results.target: ClaimNb per policy (capped at 4; claims without a recorded amount not counted), with log(Exposure) offset; rates are claims per policy-year

modelling_target.rule: claims with no recorded amount are not counted (ClaimNb set to 0); ClaimNbCapped keeps the count

split.method: random, stratified on ClaimNb > 0 (sklearn train_test_split, twice)

out_of_time.reason: freMTPL2 has no date or policy-year field, so an out-of-time test is impossible. Train, validation and test are random draws from the same period; the test metrics do not show how the models would hold up on a later year.

glm.type: Poisson GLM, log link, offset log(Exposure) (statsmodels IRLS)

lgbm.type: LightGBM objective=poisson, init_score = log(Exposure) + log(train claim frequency)

preferred_model.name: lgbm
preferred_model.rule: lower mean Poisson deviance on the validation split

recorded_claim_count_sensitivity.treatment: claims without a recorded amount kept as claims (target = ClaimNbCapped)
recorded_claim_count_sensitivity.estimates: point estimates on the test split, no bootstrap (sensitivity check, not a headline metric)

grouped_split_sensitivity.method: sklearn GroupShuffleSplit on the nine rating features (identical vectors stay in one split), seed 42, 60/20/20 of groups, not stratified; both frequency models refitted with the headline settings
grouped_split_sensitivity.estimates: point estimates per model; paired bootstrap 95% CI for LightGBM minus GLM

explainability.method: shap.TreeExplainer on the LightGBM frequency booster; values in log claims-per-year units

risk_bands.method: quantiles of the model's predictions on its training split
risk_bands.population: every policy in the training split
risk_bands.rule: a score equal to a cut-off goes to the higher band

scenario_sanity_checks.method: shift one feature by step on every test policy that stays inside the training range (others are skipped, never clipped); a violation is a prediction that moves against the expected direction

checks.why: A higher bonus-malus level records a worse claims history, so predicted claim frequency should not fall when it rises.

stability.reason: PSI needs a time field. freMTPL2 has no date or policy-year field, so an out-of-time test is impossible. Train, validation and test are random draws from the same period; the test metrics do not show how the models would hold up on a later year.

out_of_time_test.reason: freMTPL2 has no date or policy-year field, so an out-of-time test is impossible. Train, validation and test are random draws from the same period; the test metrics do not show how the models would hold up on a later year.

limitations: freMTPL2 has no date or policy-year field, so an out-of-time test is impossible. Train, validation and test are random draws from the same period; the test metrics do not show how the models would hold up on a later year.
Population stability (PSI) across time is not measured, for the same reason.

The data has no customer or vehicle identifier beyond IDpol, so the same insured risk can sit in train and test: 26.5% of test policies share every rating feature with a training policy. grouped_split_sensitivity refits both frequency models on a split grouped on the nine rating features (0.0% shared): LightGBM minus GLM mean Poisson deviance is -0.0108 [-0.0123, -0.0093] there against -0.0091 [-0.0107, -0.0075] on the random split, so the conclusion of the model comparison does not depend on identical risks sitting in both train and test.

The frequency target counts only claims with a recorded amount (see docs/insurance_data_notes.md), so frequency numbers are not directly comparable with published freMTPL2 results that use the raw ClaimNb.
LightGBM hyperparameters were fixed in advance and not tuned; only the number of trees is chosen, by early stopping on the validation split.

The validation split that early-stops LightGBM is also the one that chooses between GLM and LightGBM, which slightly favours LightGBM in that choice. The paired comparison on the untouched test split is the unbiased check of the choice; a cleaner design would early-stop on a separate fold of the training data.
Claim amounts are capped at the 99.5th percentile of training claims, so expected loss is on a capped basis with no large-loss loading.
Results are measured on public historical data from one French motor portfolio. They say nothing about performance on any other portfolio or in production.

results.dataset: freMTPL2sev (OpenML 41215) joined to freMTPL2freq on IDpol
results.target: average capped claim amount per policy with claim amounts; weight = number of claim amounts

large_loss_cap.computed_on: individual claim amounts of the training split

glm.type: Gamma GLM, log link, var_weights = number of claims (statsmodels IRLS)

lgbm.type: LightGBM objective=gamma, weight = number of claims, init_score = log(train mean severity)

preferred_model.name: glm
preferred_model.rule: lower mean Gamma deviance on the validation split

expected_loss.definition: predicted loss per policy = predicted frequency (claims/year) x exposure (years) x predicted severity (capped amount per claim); totals over all test policies
expected_loss.basis: capped claim amounts; claims without a recorded amount are not counted on either side (see data_quality.modelling_target). On the few policies whose number of amounts differs from the capped claim count, observed loss includes every recorded amount (see data_quality.linkage.n_policies_where_severity_rows_differ_from_modelling_claimnb)
